meta: Nicolas Lancret's La Camargo Dancing, about 1730, once owned by Frederick the Great and later given to the National Gallery of Art.
about: A woman in a white silk gown embroidered with flowers dances with a partner in a red coat on a woodland path while musicians and elegantly dressed onlookers gather around them. The painting belonged to Frederick II, King of Prussia, at Potsdam. It then passed down in the Hohenzollern family to Kaiser Wilhelm II. In December 1927 it was sold through a Berlin dealer to Duveen Brothers, and Andrew W. Mellon bought it in April 1928. Mellon's charitable trust gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1937.

meta: Giovanni Bellini's profile portrait of Giovanni Emo, about 1475 to 1480, once in the Brownlow collection at Ashridge Park.
about: A man in profile faces left, wearing a blue hat and a gold brocade robe over a red undergarment against a dark ground. The portrait was with a Dr. Pellegrini in Venice until 1786, when Sir Abraham Hume bought it. It then went by inheritance through his family to the earls Brownlow at Ashridge Park. Hume's printed catalogue listed it as a portrait of Bartolomeo Cogliani or Coleoni. After the Brownlow sale in London in 1923, the dealer Duveen sold it to the Kress Foundation, which gave it to the National Gallery of Art.
dimensions:
painted surface: 46.9 x 32.6 cm (18 7/16 x 12 13/16 in.)
overall size: 48.9 x 34.6 cm (19 1/4 x 13 5/8 in.)
framed: 67.3 x 54 x 6.7 cm (26 1/2 x 21 1/4 x 2 5/8 in.)

meta: Guilliam van Nieulandt's 1602 landscape of Roman ruins with Rebecca and Eliezer at the well, now in the Rijksmuseum.
about: Hilly country filled with many figures and scattered Roman ruins forms the setting for the meeting of Rebecca and Eliezer. The Rijksmuseum identifies the ruins as the Temple of Vespasian, the Temple of Saturn and the Temple of Minerva in Nerva's Forum. Women gather around water jars at the center. Before it reached the museum, the painting was probably in the collection of Hendrik van Heteren in The Hague and then in that of his son Adriaan Leonard van Heteren.

meta: Frank Duveneck's 1876 portrait of Leslie Pease Barnum, a loosely brushed bearded sitter in a dark felt hat.
about: A bearded man in a dark felt hat and a white ruff collar turns three-quarters toward the viewer against a shadowed background. The brushwork is loose. The sitter, Leslie Pease Barnum, left the portrait to his sister Louise Barnum Robbins in Adrian, Michigan, and in 1918 it went to his niece in Chicago. In 1919 it was sold to the collector Thomas B. Clarke of New York. The Mellon trust bought it with the Clarke collection and gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1942.

meta: William Stanley Haseltine's Marina Piccola, Capri, about 1858, kept by the artist's family in Rome until about 1930.
about: A small rocky cove holds wooden boats on a pebbled shore, one draped with white cloth, and a natural stone arch frames the turquoise water. Laundry dries on a rooftop above low stone buildings. The oil study, painted on paper laid on canvas, stayed with Haseltine and then with his estate at the Palazzo Altieri in Rome until about 1930. His daughter Helen Haseltine Plowden then owned it in New York. She gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1953.
dimensions:
overall (paper support): 30.5 x 47 cm (12 x 18 1/2 in.)
overall (fabric support): 31.7 x 48 cm (12 1/2 x 18 7/8 in.)
framed: 48.9 x 65.4 x 10.2 cm (19 1/4 x 25 3/4 x 4 in.)

meta: Plate XV of William Chambers's Designs of Chinese Buildings, Furniture, Dresses, Machines and Utensils, about 1750, showing tableware.
about: Eight objects sit in three tiers on this engraved plate, several of them decorated with motifs from nature such as lizards, fish and bamboo. The top tier has a vase, a three-legged burner and a vase shaped like two joined fish. Below, a teapot takes the form of a seated monkey, and another teapot resembles a piece of fruit. At the bottom, a candlestick is wound with a lizard and vines. Beside it are a teapot with bamboo motifs and a candlestick with ecclesiastic motifs. The plate is numbered XV.

meta: Pieter Jansz Quast's 1634 small panel of a surgeon examining an old man's foot while another patient has a stone cut from his head.
about: In an interior, a surgeon looks at an old man's foot. A metal jug and a shaving bowl stand on the floor at the right. At the left another man has a stone cut from his head, and a woman sits beside him. A skull rests on a book in the left foreground, and in the background a cupboard holds a figure of a saint. Quast signed the panel PQ in a ligated monogram, below the stool.

meta: William Henry Hunt's watercolor of the Green Drawing Room of the Earl of Essex at Cassiobury, made about 1820.
about: A woman in a blue dress sits at a piano in a green drawing room, with a small dog in the foreground on the right. The Cooper Hewitt describes a sky-patterned ceiling with a trompe l'oeil eagle holding the central chandelier, and dark green wall covering and curtains to match. The room includes wood carvings by Grinling Gibbons. Paintings by Turner flank the door, and the one on the right is The Thames at Walton Bridge. Bronze statuettes on pediments by the fireplace are attributed to Boulle himself, and mounted porcelain vases stand on Boulle-style cabinets. The table and chairs are in the Louis XV style.

meta: William Beechey's portrait of Lieutenant-General Sir Thomas Picton, about 1815 to 1817, one of four recorded versions.
about: A gray-haired man in a red military coat with gold braid and a high black collar wears several star-shaped orders and a blue sash across his chest. He is Lieutenant-General Sir Thomas Picton. Beechey painted four recorded versions. He kept one, which the Duke of Wellington bought at the sale after the artist's death and which is now at Apsley House in London. A Mr. Hall bought another for fifty guineas, the price of the original. The gallery's provenance note judges the Washington picture inferior to the Apsley House version, which is more solidly modeled and more firmly drawn.

meta: Jean-Étienne Liotard's 1745 pastel on parchment of Princess Karoline Luise of Hesse-Darmstadt, shown at an easel.
about: A young woman in a white silk gown with red ribbon trim sits at an easel with a stick in her hand, working on a blank sheet, and glances back toward the viewer. A chair draped in blue velvet with gold embroidery stands beside her. The sitter is Princess Karoline Luise of Hesse-Darmstadt. The Kunsthalle Karlsruhe calls Liotard a master of pastel. He is known for careful execution and finely blended surfaces. Pastel suited a lifelike rendering of skin especially well, the museum says.

meta: Fra Angelico's Madonna of Humility, about 1430, with the angel's greeting Ave Maria written in the Virgin's halo.
about: A kneeling Madonna in a blue mantle and red robe cradles the Christ Child against a gold brocade patterned with red swirls and black stars. Two angels in blue lean in from the upper corners. The words AVE MARIA GRATIA PLENA, the angel's greeting from the Gospel of Luke, are written in the Virgin's halo. The panel came from an Italian collection or dealer. Edward Steinkopff of Sussex acquired it in the late 19th century, and it passed to his daughter Mary Margaret, later Baroness Seaforth. It was given to the National Gallery of Art in 1937.
dimensions:
painted surface: 60.7 x 45.2 cm (23 7/8 x 17 13/16 in.)
support: 62.8 x 47.2 cm (24 3/4 x 18 9/16 in.)

meta: Agnolo Bronzino's Virgin and Child with Saint Elizabeth and Saint John the Baptist, about 1540 to 1545, set in a mountain landscape.
about: The Virgin Mary dominates the composition. Standing on her lap, the Christ Child takes a garland of flowers from his head and grasps a reed cross, which foreshadows the Crucifixion. The infant Saint John the Baptist, carrying the baptismal bowl, offers him a bunch of wild strawberries. The Getty reads the strawberries as a sign of Christ's fruitful and righteous life and also as a reminder of the blood spilled in the Passion. Behind Mary, an elderly Saint Elizabeth, John's mother, looks down over her shoulder.

meta: Pieter Claesz's Still Life with Peacock Pie, 1627, signed with a monogram on a knife blade and bought by the National Gallery of Art in 2013.
about: A roasted fowl, a pie crowned with a preserved peacock with its tail spread, and a pewter jug sit on a white tablecloth beside a glass of wine. Peaches and apples fill a blue and white porcelain bowl. Claesz put his initials PC and the date on the blade of a knife. The picture was probably acquired in 1827 by a private collector in England and stayed in the family until a Sotheby's sale in London in 1999. A consortium of dealers bought it, and it went to James X. Mullen of Boston. The National Gallery of Art bought it in 2013.
credit_line: The Lee and Juliet Folger Fund

meta: Henri Gervex's 1876 oil study for his Autopsy at the Hôtel-Dieu, given to the National Gallery of Art by the Knoxville Academy of Medicine.
about: In a dimly lit room, three figures in dark aprons stand around a nude body laid on a wooden table under hanging lamps. This is Henri Gervex's study for his painting Autopsy at the Hôtel-Dieu. The sheet is signed in red at the lower left, and the signature is underlined. Dr. P. Herbert Acuff of Knoxville acquired the study in Italy about 1950. After his death three Knoxville doctors bought it from his estate and gave it in 1957 to the Knoxville Academy of Medicine. The academy gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 2006.
credit_line: Gift of the Knoxville Academy of Medicine, Knoxville, Tennessee

meta: John Crome's Moonlight on the Yare, about 1816 to 1817, shown at the Franco-British Exhibition in London in 1908.
about: A river reflects a rising moon beneath a heavy, cloudy sky. Two windmills stand on the far bank beside a large tree on the left. The picture belonged to Kirkman Hodgson of Sevenoaks and then to his son Robert. By 1908 it was with H. Darell Brown in London, and it was included in that year's Franco-British Exhibition. It was later sold at Christie's, passed to Sir Arthur Howard, and then went to Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon, who gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1983.

meta: Henri Lehmann's Woman of the Orient, 1837, a seated woman on a balcony above the sea, signed and dated in Paris.
about: A seated woman in a patterned blue and gold silk dress looks over her shoulder from a balcony above a calm sea. Red drapery frames the right edge. Lehmann inscribed it at the upper right with the German form of his name, Heinrich, the year 1837 and the place, Paris. It was in a private collection in Barcelona until it was sold there at auction in June 2018. The dealer Didier Aaron in Paris handled it, and the National Gallery of Art bought it a year later.

meta: Thomas Wilmer Dewing's Lady with a Lute, 1886, bought from the artist in 1889 by Smith College.
about: A woman in profile sits on a wooden bench in a green gown with a pale yellow-green collar, playing a lute with her eyes lowered. She emerges softly from a deep, dark background. Dewing signed the picture T W Dewing and dated it 86. Smith College bought it directly from him in 1889 and called it A Lute Player. Gimbel Brothers later sold it at auction in New York, and Dr. and Mrs. Walter Timme of Cold Spring owned it before they left it to the National Gallery of Art in 1978.
credit_line: Gift of Dr. and Mrs. Walter Timme

meta: Henri Edmond Cross's Calanque des Antibois, 1891 to 1892, a sunlit Mediterranean inlet later owned by John Hay Whitney.
about: A sunlit Mediterranean inlet shows orange and violet rocks with two small boats drawn up on the shore. Cross signed it at the lower right. The picture was in Cross's estate sale at the Hôtel Drouot in Paris in 1921, and it passed through dealers including Léopold Zborowski and Bernheim-Jeune. John Hay Whitney of Manhasset, New York, bought it in 1950. His charitable trust gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1982.

meta: Meindert Hobbema's The Travelers, a wooded landscape with a watermill and two riders, signed and dated in the 1660s.
about: A large oak dominates the left foreground beside a timber-framed watermill with a red tiled roof and a turning waterwheel. Two riders on horseback travel a sandy road with their dogs. The picture belonged by 1829 to Gosen Geurt Alberda van Dyksterhuys at his château in Groningen. Sold in Amsterdam and then in Paris, it reached the English collector William Williams Hope and later William Ward, first earl of Dudley, who owned it at Witley Court by 1871.

meta: Martin Engelbrecht's Carnival of Venice, about 1730, a hand-colored paper peep-show of dancers in front of the Doges' Palace.
about: Costumed figures in bright colors dance and walk across a paved square in this hand-colored peep-show. The Palace of the Doges stands on the right and the library on the left. The museum also lists the campanile of Saint Mark's, the Mint and a church. Cut-out figures and layered architecture make up the stage. The right edge of each section is taped to a folding cardboard mount, and parts g and h are cross members.

meta: Jean Le Pautre's Designs for Friezes, 1640, a print with a boar hunt above and a stag hunt below.
about: Two bands of hunters run across this print, which gives designs for friezes. In the upper band, classical figures hunt a wild boar among oak trees, with men carrying spears, dogs and a centaur. Below, they hunt a stag, again with spears and dogs. The museum notes an agitated sense of movement in both bands, and that is the main thing to look at here.
